item.title: VAT increase for additional pensions: 49% opposed in the first poll
item.description: 49% against, 46% in favour and 5% undecided.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 49% against, 46% in favour and 5% undecided. - VAT +0.4 points to finance the extra AHV payment. - The additional payment starts in December 2026. - Detection conducted from 5 to 18 October.
## Key facts - SRG → first representative survey - Conducted by → gfs.bern, October 5-18 - Proposal to → increase VAT by 0.4 percentage points - Result → 49% against, 46% in favour, 5% undecided - Extra payment → from December 2026
### A result without a net advantage 49% of eligible voters oppose the increase in VAT intended to finance an extra annual payment of the state pension. 46% support it, while 5% are undecided. The gap of three percentage points falls within the margin of error of the survey: the first available picture therefore describes a close competition, not an already defined outcome.
The survey is SRG's first representative survey on the project. gfs.bern conducted it from 5 to 18 October and the survey was published this week. The source presents the result on the total number of eligible voters.
### What the proposal funds Two years ago, Swiss voters approved a 13th annual payment under the AVS/AHV, the old-age and survivors' insurance scheme indicated in the source under the acronym AHV. Now the Federal Council and Parliament are proposing to increase VAT by 0.4 percentage points to finance that additional benefit. The extra payment is associated with the start expected in December 2026.
The sequence separates two steps: the approval cited by the source concerns the additional annual payment; the measure now assessed in the survey is instead its financing through VAT. The survey does not present this distinction as an acquired result on the tax increase: it records the positions detected in the indicated period. The data therefore concerns the support for the increase in VAT intended to finance the service, not a new approval of the payment already decided. The source keeps the benefit and its coverage distinct.
The statement adds a caution: since the gap falls within the margin of error, the numerical distance is not enough to clearly separate the two sides. The 5% share and the fact that the campaign has just begun complete the initial picture, without turning this first survey into a forecast. ## Age, income and topics compared
### The distribution of consensus The national result is not distributed equally between age groups. Older voters are more likely to support the VAT increase, while younger voters overwhelmingly reject it; the middle age group is divided. Support is strongest among those who will benefit from the extra payment when it begins in December 2026. The source describes these guidelines, without providing a separate percentage for each band.
Income weighs less. Support and opposition are broadly balanced across income groups. Belonging to a party, however, clearly changes the picture, even if the quotas attributed to individual political forces are not indicated in the material provided.
| Factor | Indication of source | |---|---| | Age | More support among the elderly, more opposition among the young | | Intermediate range | Divided orientations | | Income | Balanced support and opposition | | Party affiliation | Marked difference | | Beneficiaries of the extra | Stronger support |
### When reasons count The clearest part of the survey concerns the arguments against it. All three tested get clear majorities. The most persuasive argues that AHV funding gaps should be closed with structural reforms, not higher taxes and levies. The source indicates a later state pension age as a central element.
The favorable arguments are less strong. 54% consider the VAT increase fair because it would guarantee the contribution of all generations. The idea that the measure represents a reasonable compromise, however, does not reach the majority, despite being the one with the greatest influence on voting intentions.
The comparison is useful because it separates the judgment on the proposal from the reaction to the reasons given to support it. The source says that, taken together, the favorable arguments garner less support than the proposal itself. It is therefore incorrect to read the 54% on equity as a percentage of overall support for the increase: it measures a specific topic, while the survey also separates voting intentions and judgment on other topics. ## A margin still open
### Two different measures of uncertainty The survey presents a useful distinction between declared indecision and unconsolidated choice. The 5% indicated in the initial framework includes voters classified as undecided. Later, however, the source states that 46% of those entitled have not yet reached a final decision. This second quota includes both those who lean towards one of the two sides and those who do not know how they will vote. The number coincides with the favourable percentage of the first figure, but the definition is different: 46% of the summary measures the declared support, while the broader 46% measures the absence of a firm choice.
This distinction reduces the risk of reading the result as an immutable block. The source points out that the campaign has just begun and that opinion may still change considerably. The data from the first survey should therefore be interpreted as an initial photograph, not as a prediction of the outcome.
### A campaign that can change the picture As the campaign progresses, voters usually move closer to the position taken by the Federal Council and Parliament on government proposals. For supporters of the increase, however, the race is starting on difficult terms: the contest is close, opponents’ arguments are strong and purchasing-power concerns remain.
Support from voters over the age of 65 introduces an element of compensation. Their above-average participation could prove to be important, according to the source. This data adds a variable to the comparison between orientations by age: the survey describes attitude, while attendance can affect the actual weight of that group.
Concerns about purchasing power, that is, the cost of living, are cited as an obstacle, but the source does not offer an individual calculation of the effect of the increase. In the material provided, the perimeter remains that of the AVS/AHV: there is no comparison with the LPP/BVG nor a breakdown of the results for Cantons. The available tax data remains the increase of 0.4 percentage points of VAT and its financing purpose; it is not translated into an expense per person or family. To follow the Swiss pension: pensione e AVS

item.title: EUR/CHF exchange rate around 0,92 on October 23, 2026
item.description: EUR/CHF around 0,92 as of October 23, 2026 One Swiss franc is worth approximately 1,09 euros The franc regains strength after a temporary weakening
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - EUR/CHF around 0,92 as of October 23, 2026 - A Swiss franc is worth approximately 1,09 euros - The franc regains strength after a temporary weakening - Geopolitics, investors, and interest rates are among the factors to watch
## Key facts | Term | Value | |---|---| | Change | EUR/CHF around 0.92 | | Date | October 23, 2026 | | Conversion indicated | 1 CHF is worth approximately 1.09 EUR | | Movement | Resumption of appreciation of the franc | | Impact described | Favorable level for those who receive income in CHF and convert it into EUR | | Variables | Geopolitical tensions, institutional investors, interest rates | | Institution | Swiss National Bank (SNB/SNB) |
On October 23, 2026, the EUR/CHF pair stood at approximately 0.92; in more immediate terms, this equates to around 1.09 euros for one Swiss franc. The price signals that the Swiss currency has started to strengthen against the euro after a temporary weakening.
The exchange rate level is described as particularly advantageous for those who receive their income in francs and convert it into euros. It is therefore a reference to the relationship between currency received and currency obtained, not the quantification of a salary. Since neither the sum to be converted nor the frequency of the operation are specified, the data only indicates a favorable exchange rate trend and does not allow the earnings of a single person to be estimated.
### From the recent data to the question about the next few months
The open question concerns the residual potential of the franc. After the recovery observed, the question is whether the currency has already expressed its full potential or can continue to appreciate, approaching new records or new historical highs in the coming months. They are hypothetical formulas: the source does not set a numerical objective and does not indicate a threshold to be reached.
To examine this possibility, the analysis brings together three areas: the behavior of institutional investors, the international geopolitical framework and the decisions of the Swiss National Bank. Interest rates are part of the variables mentioned, but in the text provided there is no specific level nor a concrete decision by the institution.
The scope of the news therefore remains clear. A strengthening against the euro is documented and the possibility of a further rise is indicated; however, no certain trajectory is promised. The date of 23 October 2026 is the reference for the price, while the horizon of the next few months belongs to the scenario to be evaluated. The distinction avoids confusing a photograph of the market with a forecast: the first data is observed, the second is presented as an eventuality. ## Reading the same exchange rate from two sides
The EUR/CHF value of around 0,92 and the indication of 1,09 euros for each franc are not two conflicting quotations. They are two ways of making the same currency relationship understandable: the first is the figure expressed as EUR/CHF, the second is the rounded inverse ratio. Starting from 0,92, the calculation 1 ÷ 0,92 returns approximately 1,087; rounded to two decimal places, it becomes 1,09. The time reference remains the same: October 23, 2026.
| Reading | Reported figure | |---|---| | EUR/CHF quotation | Around 0,92 as of October 23, 2026 | | Indicated inverse ratio | One Swiss franc is worth approximately 1,09 euros | | Effect described by the source | Favorable level for those who receive payments in CHF and convert them into EUR |
Reading it in both directions is useful because the text discusses people with income in francs who need to convert it into euros. If one starts from the franc, the figure provided by the source is 1,09 euros per unit; if one starts from the euro, the reported quotation is around 0,92 in the EUR/CHF ratio. The direction of the conversion changes how the number is read, not the fact described: the level is considered favorable for those who receive CHF and convert it into EUR.
This is the concrete comparison that the material allows. No salary amount, number of conversions, or numerical comparison with the period of temporary weakening is available. Therefore, the relationship between the two figures can be explained, but no individual result in euros can be attributed to that movement. The reference to new records is also not accompanied by an estimate: there is no target value against which to compare 0,92.
The methodological point also matters editorially. An observed strengthening and a possible new high belong to two different time frames: the first is linked to the recorded quotation, the second to the coming months. Separating the two time frames avoids presenting the second indication as an already established target. ## The safe-haven role
The source attributes part of the franc's strength to its role as a safe-haven currency. When economic or geopolitical uncertainty increases, international investors tend to seek assets considered relatively safe. The Swiss franc is described as one of the historic destinations for this capital.
According to the analysis, the franc's reputation as a safe-haven currency is supported by the political stability of the Swiss Confederation, the strength of its institutions, the credibility of its monetary policy, and the traditional prudence in managing public finances. These factors help explain demand for the currency, but they do not constitute a guarantee against every exchange-rate movement.
### The limit of protection
International tensions have refocused attention on defensive currencies and encouraged renewed interest in the franc. As long as the international environment remains characterized by uncertainty, demand for instruments considered safe could continue to support it. But the text also sets a limit: a safe-haven currency is not immune to fluctuations. The franc can weaken significantly when risk appetite improves in the markets.
The variables highlighted in the analysis remain open: the behavior of institutional investors, geopolitical developments, interest rates, and decisions by the Swiss National Bank. However, the material provided does not include specific positioning by major investors, figures on flows, interest-rate levels, or decisions already adopted by the Swiss National Bank. For this reason, the analysis supports a conditional interpretation: demand for safety as a possible source of support, greater risk appetite as a possible source of weakening, without turning either scenario into a certain forecast.
The result is a picture with potential support and an explicit limitation. The source does not allow the safe-haven reputation to be turned into a numerical forecast for the coming months. To compare the relationship between the two currencies, CHF/EUR comparator is available.

## TL;DR - The 29 November vote remains uncertain regarding AVS and war materiel - VAT for the 13th pension: 46% yes, 49% no - War materiel: 49% opposed, 41% in favor - gfs.bern poll conducted from 5 to 18 October
## Key facts - Voting day → 29 November - Institute → gfs.bern - Mandate → SSR - Survey period → 5–18 October - OASI financing → 46% yes, 49% no, 5% undecided - War materiel → 41% yes, 49% no, 10% undecided - Taxation of married couples → 55% yes, 34% no, 11% undecided - Fireworks → 69% yes, 29% no, 2% undecided
### Two issues still unresolved Six weeks before the 29 November vote, the first poll conducted by the gfs.bern institute on behalf of SSR paints a divided picture. The survey was conducted between 5 and 18 October and published today. The news item, marked Keystone-ATS, summarizes voting intentions on the four items on the ballot.
Additional OASI financing through an increase in VAT remains in the balance. 46% of respondents are in favor, 49% opposed and 5% have not yet decided. Among SP supporters, the yes vote reaches 60%, while it stands at 58% among Greens and Centre supporters and at 56% among GLP supporters. The SVP, by contrast, records 68% no votes and the FDP 54%.
The demographic profile further differentiates voting intentions. Among those aged 18 to 39, support for the financing is 35%; among those over 65, it rises to 55%. By sex, men reject the proposal more strongly, with 52% opposed. Among women, the figures are balanced: 47% are in favor and 47% opposed. The difference between the linguistic regions is smaller: approval reaches 45% in German-speaking Switzerland and 47% in both Romandy and Italian-speaking Switzerland.
The revision of the Federal Act on War Material also has no clear majority. 49% say they are opposed, 41% are in favor and 10% remain undecided. Those aged 18 to 39 are more opposed to the proposal, with 54% voting no, while among those over 65, the yes vote reaches 60%. By gender, 57% of men support easing the rules on exports of war materiel, compared with 41% of women. By language, support is 53% in German-speaking Switzerland, 37% in Romandy and 45% in Italian-speaking Switzerland. ## Comparison between the two uncertain proposals
### Different margins in the same poll The arithmetic comparison between the two proposals shows two close, but not identical, situations. For AVS financing, no votes exceed yes votes by 3 percentage points: 49% versus 46%, with 5% undecided. For war materiel, the gap is 8 points: 49% opposed versus 41% in favor, while 10% are undecided. These are differences calculated based on the values published by the poll, not definitive voting results.
The distribution by age follows a similar direction in both cases, but with different indicators. For AVS financing, support rises from 35% among 18-39-year-olds to 55% among over-65s: a difference of 20 points. For war materiel, by contrast, no prevails among younger people at 54%, while yes prevails among over-65s at 60%. The figure does not measure the same response in the two proposals, but indicates how age separates voting intentions in both issues.
| Profile | AVS financing | War materiel | |---|---|---| | Age | 18-39-year-olds: 35% yes; over-65s: 55% yes | 18-39-year-olds: 54% no; over-65s: 60% yes | | Sex | Men: 52% no; women: 47% yes and 47% no | Men: 57% yes; women: 41% yes | | Language region | German-speaking Switzerland: 45% yes; Romandy and Italian-speaking Switzerland: 47% | German-speaking Switzerland: 53% yes; Romandy: 37%; Italian-speaking Switzerland: 45% |
The regional factor also produces two different maps. For AVS financing, the difference between 45% in German-speaking Switzerland and 47% in the other two language regions is only 2 points. For war materiel, the distance between German-speaking Switzerland and Romandy is 16 points, while that between German-speaking Switzerland and Italian-speaking Switzerland is 8 points.
The political comparison follows the same line of separation. For AVS, yes votes prevail among PS, Verdi, Centro and PVL, respectively at 60%, 58%, 58% and 56%. No votes are instead 68% among UDC sympathizers and 54% among PLR sympathizers. For war materiel, Verdi and PS reject the change with 63% and 62% no votes. Support instead reaches 73% among PLR sympathizers, 65% in Centro, 60% in PVL and 57% in UDC. The source reports these distributions without indicating voters' reasons. ## The two initiatives leaning toward yes
### Fireworks: the broadest support The proposal that appears relatively less contested is the «For a restriction on fireworks» Initiative. 69% of respondents say they are in favor, 29% against, and only 2% undecided. The difference between yes and no is therefore 40 percentage points, calculated based on the survey figures.
Support remains in the majority in the political breakdown reported by the poll. Among the various party electorates cited, the shares in favor are 59%, 67%, 80%, 83% and 91%. The source therefore shows a range of 59% to 91% for this initiative, in addition to the overall figure of 69%.
The difference is also visible by gender: women support the proposal with 76% yes, compared with 60% among men. In the language regions, the initiative receives 69% in German-speaking Switzerland, 67% in French-speaking Switzerland and 61% in Italian-speaking Switzerland. By age, approval is strongest among those over 65, at 73%, while among 18- to 39-year-olds it stands at 66%.

Among the parties, the initiative receives 71% yes among Centre voters and 64% among UDC voters. In the PLR, 52% are in favor, with a still significant share undecided. The Greens and PS both stand at 40% yes, while the PVL reaches 45%.
The regional differences are more pronounced than the age-related ones. In Italian-speaking Switzerland, support reaches 65%, followed by 60% in French-speaking Switzerland and 53% in German-speaking Switzerland. By age, those in favor account for 52% among 18- to 39-year-olds, 58% among 40- to 64-year-olds and 54% among those over 65.
The overall picture described by Keystone-ATS is therefore one of two initiatives leaning toward yes, but with different levels of support, alongside two projects that are still uncertain. The available text reports voting intentions collected from October 5 to 18; it does not document the result of the vote or indicate the reasons for the choices expressed. item.title: Short-time work: the Federal Council envisages a gradual return to normality
item.description: The Federal Council intends to gradually normalize the ILR Maximum duration: 24 months until January 31, 2027 Expected growth: 1,7% in 2026 and 1,6%
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The Federal Council intends to gradually normalize ILR - Maximum duration: 24 months until January 31, 2027 - Forecast growth: 1,7% in 2026 and 1,6% in 2027 - From 2028, the waiting period returns to three days
## Key facts - Date → 21 October 2026 - Place → Bern - Instrument → short-time work compensation (STC) - Current maximum duration → 24 months - Ordinary duration → 12 months - Current waiting period → one day - Expiry of current duration → 31 January 2027 - Department in charge → EAER
On 21 October 2026, in Bern, the Federal Council discussed the framework conditions for short-time work compensation (STC). The Executive intends to gradually normalize the instrument because the economic situation has improved.
During periods of economic difficulty, short-time work helps preserve the stability of companies and employment. Through STC, unemployment insurance (UI) temporarily covers a substantial share of remuneration for hours not worked. The measure therefore concerns companies that suffer unavoidable losses of work.
### Decision and timeline
Within the limits set by law, the Federal Council can adjust the framework conditions, intervening primarily on the maximum duration for receiving STC and the waiting period. During crises, the duration is extended and the waiting period shortened; when the economic situation improves, both parameters are gradually brought back to the ordinary levels provided for by law.
For now, STC can be received for a maximum of 24 months, rather than the ordinary 12 months; the waiting period is one day, compared with the three normally provided for. The extension to 24 months remains valid until 31 January 2027. In December 2026, in light of the economic situation and the economic outlook, the Federal Council will assess whether to renew the extension from February 2027 and to what extent. It will also examine other measures to bring the duration back to the ordinary 12 months during 2027, depending on economic developments. ## The comparison between rules and economic conditions
Reading the data requires keeping separate the units used in the press release: months and days describe the parameters of ILR, while economic outlooks report annual growth rates. The comparison can be summarized as follows:
| Parameter or data | First value | Second reference | |---|---:|---:| | Maximum ILR duration | 24 months | 12 standard months | | Waiting period | one day | three days from 2028 | | Growth of the Swiss economy | 1,7% in 2026 | 1,6% in 2027 |
### Two parameters, two horizons
The maximum duration indicates the time horizon within which the benefit may be received; the waiting period, by contrast, is expressed in days. The press release describes both as framework conditions that can be modified by the Federal Council depending on the economic situation. The current rule combines a duration extended to 24 months with a waiting period reduced to one day. The return to the standard reference points is instead staggered across different deadlines: the duration will be reassessed in December 2026, while the three-day waiting period will return from 2028.
From an economic perspective, the Confederation's outlook of September 17, 2026, indicates growth of the Swiss economy of 1,7% in 2026 and 1,6% in 2027. The arithmetic difference between the two forecasts is 0,1 percentage points: 1,7% minus 1,6%. This is a comparison between two annual estimates referring to different periods.
The same source forecasts that unemployment and short-time work will continue to decline. These data, together with the positive outlook, give the Federal Council room to begin a gradual normalization. However, the text does not present an immediate change to all the parameters: it distinguishes the assessment of the duration, scheduled for December, from the return of the three-day waiting period, set to take effect from 2028. For hours not worked, AD meanwhile continues to temporarily cover a large part of the salary payments provided for under ILR. ## Risks and next steps
The improved outlook does not eliminate the risks identified by the Confederation: geopolitical tensions, high energy prices and uncertainty over trade policy. For this reason, the Federal Council will closely monitor economic developments and maintain dialogue with the social partners and the business community.
### A decision that still depends on the data
The duration of ILR beyond January 31, 2027, has not yet been determined. In December 2026, the Federal Council will assess whether to extend the maximum duration again from February 2027, and to what extent. It will also consider further measures to return it to the standard twelve months during 2027. The assessment will take into account the economic situation at the time and the economic outlook.
The change to the waiting period will follow its own timetable. Since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, companies’ contribution to short-time work costs has been limited to one waiting day; from 2028, the “deductible” will return to the standard three days. To change the duration and waiting period, it will be necessary to amend the Ordinance on Unemployment Insurance (OADI). The Federal Council has assigned this task to the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research (DEFR); a public consultation is planned for the first months of 2027.
### Access for companies
According to the press release, short-time work will remain accessible in the future to all companies experiencing unavoidable losses of work. Companies that already benefit from ILR or intend to do so can submit the application and/or statements online via the “Short-time work application/calculation” eService on the lavoro.swiss portal. Overall, the picture points to a gradual return to the standard parameters, accompanied by an assessment of the economic situation and a public consultation.
*Source: [seco.admin.ch](https://www.seco.admin.ch/it/newnsb/UsLZDezPNQYF)*

item.title: Living in Switzerland: one in 6 spends more than a third of their income
item.description: The 16% exceeds one third of gross household income The 22% of tenants exceeds the housing threshold The 7% of homeowners exceeds the same limit
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 16% exceeds one third of gross household income - 22% of tenants exceed the housing threshold - 7% of homeowners exceed the same limit - 36% of households with up to 4000 francs exceed the threshold
## Key facts - Threshold → one third of gross household income - Survey → representative, commissioned by Comparis - Tenants above the threshold → 22% - Homeowners above the threshold → 7% - Monthly gross income up to 4000 francs → 36% above the threshold - Theoretical rate applied by banks → 5% - Source abbreviation → ATS (Keystone-ATS)
16% of respondents allocate more than one third of their gross household income to housing. This is the central finding of the representative survey commissioned by the online comparison service Comparis. The news item, introduced by the ATS abbreviation in the form Keystone-ATS, translates the percentage into an immediate formula: one in six Swiss people exceeds the threshold considered a benchmark for housing expenses.
### The comparison between tenants and homeowners
The pressure is not distributed equally. Among tenants, 22% allocate more than one third of their income to housing. Among homeowners, the share falls to 7%. The comparison shows a difference of 15 percentage points between the two groups, calculated by subtracting 7% from 22%; it does not, however, indicate the average amount paid by each household.
The source points to difficulties especially among households with low incomes. Among those whose monthly gross income does not exceed 4000 francs, 36% allocate more than one third of their income to housing. This figure concerns the group of households identified in the survey and is not extended by the source to all income brackets.
> «The so-called one-third rule is not a law of nature, but it is an important warning benchmark,» comments Harry Büsser, real estate expert at Comparis, quoted in a press release.
According to Büsser, consistently exceeding the threshold can erode the resources needed for healthcare and retirement provision and leave little room to deal with unexpected expenses. The survey, therefore, measures not only the share allocated to rent or homeownership, but also what remains in the household budget after housing costs have been paid. The reference to 5% concerns buying a home through a mortgage. Before granting financing, financial institutions generally assess affordability based on a theoretical interest rate of 5%, higher than current market levels. This is not the rate actually paid by the homeowner, but rather the theoretical parameter used in the bank's assessment.
### Affordability goes beyond the day of purchase
The bank's assessment concerns the moment when the mortgage is granted. The source warns, however, that this assessment does not guarantee that the burden will remain affordable in the following years. After the purchase, the household budget may change if an income is lost, in the event of separation, a reduction in the employment rate or retirement. Comparis therefore indicates that, in addition to the ability to bear housing costs under current conditions, the ability to cope with financial changes and unforeseen events is also relevant.
This clarifies the relationship between the 5% and the one-third rule. The former is a theoretical criterion applied by financial institutions to the affordability of the financing; the latter is defined by Büsser as an alert value for the burden of housing on gross household income. They are different quantities, and the text does not add them together, convert them into a monthly installment or indicate by how much each household exceeds the threshold.
### Other budget items
The reference to healthcare and pension costs connects the housing figure to the cost of living, but the survey does not separate these items into instruments such as LAMal/KVG, AVS/AHV or LPP/BVG. These terms help to interpret the categories mentioned in the source; however, they are not additional percentages or amounts from the survey. Comparis only points out the risk that, in the face of a consistently high housing burden, a family may have to cut back on other essential expenses. The survey does not only describe the difficulties faced by those who pay rent. The source also cautions against an immediate comparison between the monthly cost of ownership and that of renting: at first glance, owning may seem more affordable, but a considerable portion of equity remains tied up in the house or apartment. That money cannot be invested to generate a return. Maintenance, renovations and major repairs are also added to the monthly cost.
### The comparison missing from the monthly payment alone
The interpretation proposed by Comparis can be summarized as follows:
| Item | Source's indication | |---|---| | Monthly housing costs | Owning often seems more affordable than renting | | Equity | It is tied up in the house or apartment | | Alternative use of capital | It cannot be invested to generate a return | | Additional expenses | Maintenance, renovations and major repairs | | Long-term horizon | Owning may be attractive, but is not automatically more affordable |
The table does not alter the 7% figure among homeowners and does not make it possible to determine which choice is best for every family. It adds a limitation to a comparison based solely on the monthly payment or housing expenditure: the source also considers the capital tied up and the outlays that arise over time.
The text does not provide a breakdown of the percentages by canton or city. Nor does it attribute the figures to UST/BFS or SECO: it presents them as the result of a representative survey commissioned by Comparis, with the news reported by Keystone-ATS. Therefore, the 16%, 22%, 7% and 36% describe the shares indicated for the groups mentioned, but do not make it possible to reconstruct territorial differences, average amounts or changes over time.
The specialist's conclusion remains cautious: owning may prove attractive in the long term, but it is not necessarily more affordable. To read this topic alongside the other expenses incurred by households, consult cost of living in Switzerland

item.title: BNS: policy rate unchanged and moderate inflation
item.description: The SNB keeps its policy rate at 0 percent In September, the SNB abandons the exchange-rate formula Inflationary pressure is increasing only slightly
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The BNS keeps the policy rate at 0 percent - In September, the BNS abandons the wording on foreign exchange - Inflationary pressure rises only slightly - AI may affect unemployment and consumption
## Key facts - Institution: Swiss National Bank (BNS) - Location: Zurich - Decision: policy rate unchanged at 0 percent - Date of the rate decision: September 24 - Market: foreign exchange market - Risk: second-round effects of energy prices - Topic: artificial intelligence and the labor market
### The September decision On September 24, the Swiss National Bank kept its policy rate at 0 percent. According to the summary of the monetary policy discussion published Thursday, the Governing Board of the BNS does not currently consider it necessary to increase its readiness to operate in the foreign exchange market.
The document concerns the September rate decision and makes explicit the change in wording compared with June. At that time, the BNS was still declaring a greater readiness to operate in the foreign exchange market. In September, it removed that indication, considering it no longer necessary in the current context.
The rationale indicated in the minutes is limited in scope. The BNS notes only a slight increase in medium-term inflationary pressure and considers the second-round effects related to the rise in energy prices barely perceptible. So far, the summary adds, there are few signs that the increases are being passed on to other goods and services or to wages.
The reference to oil adds a specific condition to the assessment: the longer prices remain at high levels, the greater the risk of second-round effects. The BNS does not describe these effects as already widespread; it presents them as barely perceptible, with few signs of transmission to other goods and services or to wages.
The reference to foreign-exchange readiness therefore describes the central bank's assessment of the need to be ready to intervene. The news concerns both the policy rate, which remained at 0 percent, and the language the BNS uses to assess its position on foreign exchange. The minutes also open a second chapter, devoted to the possible effects of artificial intelligence on the labor market, still without a definitive assessment. ### The comparison between June and September The comparison documented in the summary concerns above all the wording on readiness in foreign exchange. For June, the source reports an indication of greater readiness; for September, it states that the wording was abandoned. As for the rate, however, the explicit figure is the one from September 24, when the level remained at 0 percent.
| Time | BNS indication | | --- | --- | | June | Greater readiness to intervene in the foreign-exchange market | | September | The wording is abandoned; greater readiness is not considered necessary | | September 24 | Policy rate unchanged at 0 percent |
This reading separates two aspects of the decision. On the one hand, the BNS does not currently see the need to maintain the previous wording on its readiness to intervene in the foreign-exchange market. On the other, the policy rate remains unchanged. The summary does not report an actual intervention in the foreign-exchange market and does not present a rate forecast: it documents an assessment of readiness and a rate level.
### Energy prices and inflationary pressure The second comparison concerns the nature of the risks identified. Medium-term inflationary pressure is described as rising only slightly. The second-round effects of higher energy prices, by contrast, are barely perceptible. The summary therefore distinguishes between the rise in energy prices and their possible pass-through to other prices or wages: so far, there are few signs of this pass-through.
The BNS does not rule out the risk. The minutes specify that the longer oil prices remain at elevated levels, the greater the risk of second-round effects will be. The reference is temporal and conditional: the source does not indicate how long prices will remain high and does not quantify either inflation or the impact on goods, services, or wages.
As for the cost of living, the document does not propose a standalone indicator; instead, it refers to goods, services, and wages. The clearest point, therefore, is the combination of an unchanged policy rate and more cautious wording on foreign-exchange readiness. The document records the decision made in September and the risk associated with oil prices remaining elevated, without turning it into a forecast. ### AI appears in the minutes In addition to prices and exchange rates, the SNB discussed the possible effects of artificial intelligence on the labor market. According to the summary, the spread of AI could result in higher structural unemployment and a slowdown in consumption. The document does not, however, offer a definitive assessment: it is still too early for a conclusive evaluation.
This passage has a different scope from the one on energy inflation. In the first case, the SNB describes still limited signs that energy price increases are being passed on to other goods, services and wages. In the second, it sets out a possible development linked to the evolution of AI: higher structural unemployment and weaker consumption. The source does not establish that these effects have already occurred, nor does it link them to an immediate monetary policy measure.
### What the text documents and what it does not document The summary discloses several specific points: the decision, in September, to drop the wording on greater readiness in the foreign-exchange market; the policy rate at 0 percent on September 24; the slight increase in medium-term inflationary pressure; and the still limited perception of second-round effects from energy prices. With regard to oil, the risk increases if prices remain high for longer. With regard to AI, however, there is no conclusive assessment.
The content does not report a new decision on the policy rate, an announced foreign-exchange intervention, a quantification of inflation, an unemployment figure or a forecast for consumption. Nor does it provide operational guidance for businesses, workers or households. The text remains a summary of the monetary policy discussion relating to the September decision, published on Thursday, and presents the SNB's assessments without turning the risks described into already established outcomes.
The caution therefore concerns both the position on exchange rates and the interpretation of future developments. In the first case, the SNB does not consider the greater readiness signaled in June necessary; in the second, it acknowledges that AI could affect the labor market but defers a definitive assessment. These are the two explicit limits that emerge from the document.

item.title: Adjustment of LPP survivors’ and disability pensions from 1 January 2027
item.description: From January 1, 2027, annuities will be adjusted to prices.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - From January 1, 2027, pensions will be adjusted in line with prices. - 2,1% for entitlements arising in 2023. - 1% after one year for pensions adjusted in 2026. - 1,2% after two years for those adjusted in 2025.
## Key facts - What → survivors' and disability pensions under mandatory LPP - Publication → October 22, 2026 - Effective date → January 1, 2027 - Entitlement arising in 2023 → 2,1% - Subsequent adjustments → 1% after January 1, 2026; 1,2% after January 1, 2025
### The measure announced in Bern
The announcement, issued in Bern on October 22, 2026, provides that from January 1, 2027, the amount of survivors' and disability pensions under mandatory occupational pension provision will follow price trends. The measure will affect both benefits undergoing their first adjustment and benefits already adjusted previously.
Within the mandatory occupational pension scheme, adjustments to survivors' and disability pensions periodically follow the development of the consumer price index until the ordinary retirement age. The first takes place three years after entitlement begins; subsequent ones are carried out in conjunction with AVS updates, generally at two-year intervals.
For pensions for which entitlement arose in 2023, the announced rate is 2,1%. The calculation uses the consumer price index for September 2023, equal to 99,4159, and that for September 2026, equal to 101,4737. The stated base is December 2025 = 100.
As part of the increase in AVS pensions planned for 2027, the document addresses these cases separately. For pensions whose first adjustment dates back to January 1, 2026, the new measure will take place after one year and will be 1%; the announcement also expresses the same rate as 1,0%. Those last adjusted on January 1, 2025, on the other hand, will receive the adjustment after two years, at a rate of 1,2%.
The distinction used by the source is precise: in the first group, the year in which entitlement arose matters, while in the other two the date of the last adjustment matters. The calendar therefore shows the different use of dates: for entitlement arising in 2023, the origin of the benefit is considered; for pensions adjusted in 2026 or 2025, the previous revision is considered instead. The common effective date remains January 1, 2027, while the technical basis is indicated through the indices for the respective periods. ### The comparison between the indices
The clearest figure for checking the difference between the cases is the period observed. The September 2026 value, 101,4737, is the common endpoint of the comparisons shown; the starting value and the date to which it refers vary. The table brings together the figures indicated by the source.
| Pension group | Index comparison | Common base | Rate | |---|---|---|---| | Entitlement arising in 2023 | September 2023: 99,4159 → September 2026: 101,4737 | December 2025 = 100 | 2,1% | | Adjusted for the first time on January 1, 2026 | September 2025: 100,4789 → September 2026: 101,4737 | December 2025 = 100 | 1% | | Last adjusted on January 1, 2025 | September 2024: 100,2539 → September 2026: 101,4737 | December 2025 = 100 | 1,2% |
When read as arithmetic differences in index points, the values show three distances from the September 2026 reference. There are 2,0578 points between 99,4159 and 101,4737; there are 0,9948 between 100,4789 and 101,4737; and 1,2198 between 100,2539 and 101,4737. These calculations do not alter the reported rates: they make the values being compared visible.
The first comparison covers September 2023-September 2026, while the second uses September 2025-September 2026 and the third September 2024-September 2026. The source links these periods to the dates on which the previous adjustments took effect: after one year for pensions adjusted for the first time on January 1, 2026, and after two years for those last adjusted on January 1, 2025. The criterion for the first adjustment after three years is reported separately for the mandatory scheme.
The link to the cost of living here runs through the consumer price index: the source does not express the adjustment in francs, but in relation to the change in the indices. The December 2025 = 100 base makes the values comparable, even though they refer to September in different years. The communiqué also places the two subsequent adjustments in the 2027 increase in AVS pensions, so that the occupational pension calendar is considered alongside that of AVS. ### The limit provided for by the LPP
Automatic adjustment is not provided for all pensions. If the amount exceeds the statutory minimum, the pension institution is not required to offset price developments.
The supreme governing body of the pension institution determines each year whether to adjust the pensions and sets the possible extent of the adjustment. The source refers to Art. 36 para. 2 LPP; these determinations are discussed in the pension institution's accounts or annual report. The passage distinguishes the rates indicated for the groups considered from the annual assessment provided for other situations covered by the communication.
The informational limit is equally clear: the text indicates percentages, indices and reference dates, but does not report individual amounts in francs, does not identify a single pension institution and does not indicate a specific pension. The rates of 2.1%, 1% and 1.2% can therefore be used to derive the adjustment criterion described, but not a personal amount. The note also does not provide a list of pensions that exceed the statutory minimum; that requirement remains the explicit criterion for the obligation to adjust.
The temporal scope remains that indicated in the rules described: survivors' and disability pensions under the mandatory second-pillar scheme are periodically adjusted in line with the evolution of the consumer price index until the ordinary retirement age. The communication separates this rule from cases in which the decision depends on the institution's financial capacity and on the supreme governing body.
For the overview of benefits AVS/LPP/pension.

item.title: Buying used goods in Switzerland: warranty and rules
item.description: One-year warranty, unless explicitly excluded Public land: free items are often prohibited Counterfeits across borders: possible seizure and a fee
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - One-year warranty, unless explicitly excluded - Public land: free items are often prohibited - Counterfeits across the border: possible seizure and a fee of about 100 francs - Receipt: it is better to include the seller's details
## Key facts - Guarantee at a flea market: one year in principle - Exclusion: “sold as seen” wording - Receipt: seller’s details - Public land: practice often prohibited - Border: possible fee of around 100 francs - Reference: Gabriela Baumgartner, Radio SRF 1, October 5, 2026
In principle, a one-year warranty, unless explicitly excluded, applies to the purchase of a used item at a flea market in Switzerland. The rule falls within the framework of the Code of Obligations and concerns a market that also includes secondhand shops, online platforms and items left free of charge in front of a home.
The seller may exclude the warranty. Wording such as “sold as seen” is not presented as a mere phrase of convenience: it constitutes an explicit exclusion. Anyone who accepts this condition waives the related rights. For this reason, the source recommends asking for a receipt that includes at least the seller’s details. If a dispute arises, it is necessary to be able to identify who sold the goods.
The report refers to explanations by Gabriela Baumgartner, broadcast by Radio SRF 1 on October 5, 2026. The guidance concerns both the relationship between seller and buyer and the way in which unwanted items are left.
### When a giveaway takes up the street
Leaving boxes of books, furniture or other goods marked “free” on the sidewalk or by the roadside may seem harmless. Legally, however, in numerous municipalities the act may constitute illegal dumping; when public land is occupied, it is also often prohibited.
Leaving goods to be given away in public space is not generally recognized as a right. Regulations vary from city to city: some municipalities impose strict restrictions, while others tolerate the practice only if the items do not obstruct passage and are removed quickly.
On private land, by contrast, items intended to be given away can normally be left. The person making them available no longer retains ownership, which passes to whoever collects them. The sole exception concerns items contained in bags from official used-clothing collections: they remain the property of the sponsoring organization. ## Warranty, receipt and wrong purchase
The distinction between warranty and the right of withdrawal is the point most likely to create confusion in second-hand purchases. The warranty concerns the rights connected to the purchased item and may be excluded by the seller. Withdrawal, on the other hand, concerns the possibility of changing one’s mind after the purchase has been concluded: according to the source, Swiss law does not provide for a general right of this kind.
The framework reported for the different sales channels can be summarized as follows:
| Situation | Rule indicated by the source | |---|---| | Flea market | In principle, a one-year warranty; the seller may exclude it | | “Sold as seen” formula | Explicit exclusion of the warranty; the buyer waives the related rights | | Second-hand shop | For second-hand goods, a one-year warranty instead of two | | Exclusion in a second-hand shop | Permitted if customers are informed clearly | | Return or exchange | Granted only voluntarily by the seller |
Second-hand shops are shops in every respect. Their activity therefore does not eliminate the rules governing warranties, but the source notes that many retailers exclude them completely. The condition indicated is that the information be clear to customers. In the case of flea markets, the same attention must be paid to the wording used by the seller before concluding the transaction.
### The receipt as an identifying element
Asking for a receipt does not automatically change the warranty or turn an exclusion into a right. Its function as described in the report is more practical: retaining at least the seller’s details makes it possible to know whom to contact in the event of subsequent disputes. Without identification, pursuing a claim can become problematic precisely because it would not be possible to determine who sold the goods.
The source also distinguishes the warranty from simply changing one’s mind. Someone who makes a wrong purchase cannot assume that the seller must take the goods back. There is no general obligation to accept returns, and an exchange likewise depends on the retailer’s willingness. The fact that an item is used, that it was purchased in a shop, or that the buyer has changed their mind does not, by itself, create a general right to return it.
The practical consequence described in the text is a distinction between what the seller may be required to guarantee and what they may choose to do. The warranty may be excluded when the exclusion is communicated explicitly or clearly; returns and exchanges, on the other hand, remain voluntary initiatives. For this reason, the purchase conditions and the seller’s identity carry different weight: the former define the rights connected to the warranty, while the latter makes it possible to identify the other party if a dispute arises. ## Low prices, counterfeit goods and the border
Price is one of the main reasons why second-hand markets attract buyers. However, the source urges particular caution when the price appears exceptionally advantageous. The stated criterion is not to automatically regard every bargain as suspicious, but to carefully check the condition of the item, ask the seller questions, and assess whether the price is truly plausible. If in doubt, the suggestion is to be wary; if one decides to purchase anyway, it is advisable to ask for a receipt.
### The designer handbag case
One might consider an authentic designer handbag sold for a price much lower than its market value. The person who buys it is not obliged to disclose its actual value to the seller. However, the seller could later challenge the contract if they proved that they had entered into it without knowing the item's value.
This passage shows that the source does not present a very low price as automatic proof of illegal activity or counterfeiting. Instead, it is a factor that calls for more careful checks of the item and the plausibility of the deal. The source does not indicate a numerical threshold above which the price must be considered suspicious and does not establish that every highly advantageous purchase should be refused.
### The risk for those who buy across the border
Anyone who sells stolen or counterfeit goods commits a crime; on the other hand, according to the report, anyone who in good faith buys such an item at a Swiss second-hand market does not commit a criminal offense. The most significant difficulties arise with cross-border purchases, when people visit second-hand markets in neighboring countries and then return to Switzerland.
Customs checks focus above all on counterfeit branded products. If found during an inspection, they may be seized; anyone bringing them into Switzerland may also have to pay a fee of about 100 francs. The source presents this figure as approximate, not as an amount that applies indiscriminately to every inspection, and does not indicate any additional amounts.
The border therefore marks a difference compared with a good-faith purchase made at a Swiss second-hand market. In the first case described, the buyer does not commit a criminal offense; in the second, bringing counterfeit branded products into the country may lead to seizure and a fee. Checking the item, asking the seller questions, and obtaining a receipt therefore remain central; these are measures that the source links both to protecting the buyer and to the possibility of reconstructing the purchase.
*Source: [rsi.ch](https://www.rsi.ch/info/dialogo/Mercatini-e-usato-cinque-cose-da-sapere--4155286.html)*

item.title: Emergency shutdown at the Gösgen nuclear power plant, no danger
item.description: Tuesday, around 6:40, Gösgen shut down.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Tuesday, around 6.40, Gösgen shut down. - Indicated cause: drop in electrical voltage. - The safety systems acted according to protocols. - There was no release of radioactive material.
## Key facts - Plant → Gösgen nuclear power plant - Location → canton of Solothurn - Time → Tuesday, around 6:40 - Cause → drop in electrical voltage - Owner → KKG company - Status → plant disconnected - Restart → IFSN approval
Around 6:40 on Tuesday morning, a drop in electrical voltage in the system powering the control rods caused the automatic shutdown of the Gösgen nuclear power plant in the canton of Solothurn. These components serve to regulate activity inside the reactor.
The source presents the case as a distinct sequence: first the automatic shutdown, then verification of the behavior of the safety systems, and finally the suspension of operations pending authorization. KKG, the company that owns the plant, indicated that all safety systems operated correctly and in accordance with protocols.
### The situation at present According to the report, the plant remains safe and no radioactive material leak occurred. The Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate, referred to in the source by the acronym IFSN, emphasizes the same absence of leaks.
At present, the plant remains disconnected. Operations will resume as soon as IFSN gives the go-ahead: the text thus separates the current technical status from the subsequent restart decision. ## The technical point to distinguish The report brings together three aspects that should not be confused: the electrical anomaly indicated as the cause, the plant’s automatic response and the safety check. The drop in voltage concerns the system that supplies power to the control rods; the shutdown is the response recorded by the plant; the proper operation of the safety systems, on the other hand, concerns compliance with protocols. The source adds a fourth, radiological element: no release of radioactive material.
This distinction makes the information easier to interpret without turning it into a judgment different from the one reported. The automatic shutdown is a change in the plant’s operating status. It is not described as a radioactive release, and the source explicitly says that the plant is currently safe. At the same time, the plant is not operational: it is disconnected and awaiting IFSN approval. These are therefore two compatible pieces of information that should be kept separate: declared safety and operations still suspended.
### From cause to current status | Step | What the source reports | |---|---| | Indicated cause | drop in electrical voltage | | Response | automatic shutdown | | Safety | systems compliant with protocols | | Radioactive material | no release | | Operating status | plant disconnected | | Restart | after IFSN approval |
The role of IFSN appears at two different points: the institution is mentioned in connection with the absence of a release, and its approval is necessary for the restart. KKG, on the other hand, reports the behavior of the safety systems. The source does not assign the same function to the two institutions. ## What remains documented The source stops at the situation following the shutdown. It reports that the power plant is disconnected and that operations will resume as soon as IFSN gives the go-ahead. It does not indicate when that approval will come or how long the disconnection will last. No further technical details are reported about the voltage drop or any measures taken after the shutdown. These limitations prevent adding a duration, a forecast for the restart or undocumented consequences.
### The scope of the information The available data nevertheless make it possible to establish certain points without conflating different aspects. The facility is located in the canton of Solothurn; the owner is KKG; IFSN is indicated both for confirming the absence of a leak and for the approval required for resumption. The source also reports that all safety systems operated correctly, in accordance with protocols. From an operational standpoint, however, the facility remains disconnected at the time described.
The text does not document damage, injuries, radioactivity levels, the duration of the interruption or effects on the electricity service. The verifiable information is therefore limited to the sequence reported: automatic shutdown, safety confirmed, no leak and awaiting IFSN’s approval.

## TL;DR - Partial revision of the SERV indicated on October 21, 2026 - Objective: facilitate access to SERV benefits - Reduction of burdens and simplification of products - Mandate regarding jobs and the business location unchanged
## Key facts - Date → October 21, 2026 - Place → Bern - Subject → partial revision concerning SERV - Purpose → more targeted response to the needs of Switzerland’s export-oriented economy - Mandate → preserve and create jobs; promote Switzerland as a business location
### The revision indicated in the communication The external communication published on October 21, 2026, from Bern, presents the objectives of a partial revision concerning SERV. SERV is referred to in the title as Swiss Export Risk Insurance. The text focuses on the changes being pursued and does not indicate an entry-into-force date.
The first objective is to facilitate access to SERV services. The second is to reduce the administrative burden. The third concerns the introduction and adjustment of products, which the revision aims to simplify. There are therefore three operational levers: access, compliance requirements and products. The communication links them to the possibility for SERV to tailor its intervention more precisely to the needs of Switzerland’s export-oriented economy.
For those observing the national economy, the documented point is the scope of the intervention: the source speaks of how the services operate and of the response to the needs of the exporting economy. However, it does not quantify the extent of the administrative reduction, list specific products or indicate amounts or deadlines. The text therefore describes what the revision aims to achieve, not a measure already implemented or a verified result. The fundamental mandate of SERV, the source specifies, remains unchanged. ## Two levels to distinguish The source allows a clear comparison between what the revision seeks to change and what it states it will leave unchanged. At the first level are access to benefits, administrative burdens, and the introduction or adjustment of products. At the second is SERV’s fundamental mandate: to preserve and create jobs and promote Switzerland as a business location.
| Area | What the source indicates | |---|---| | Access | Facilitate access to SERV benefits | | Administration | Reduce administrative burdens | | Products | Simplify introduction and adjustment | | Mandate | Preserve and create jobs; promote Switzerland as a business location |
The comparison does not measure a before and after: the communication does not provide initial values, expected values, or a measurement period. It does, however, make it possible to distinguish the revision of the instruments from the mandate. In editorial terms, the text presents an intervention concerning usability and the adaptation of the offering, not a redefinition of the stated purpose.
This distinction is relevant for a national reading. The relationship made explicit by the source moves from operational simplification to a more targeted response to the needs of the Swiss export-oriented economy. The effect on individual entities, sectors, or numerical results is not documented, however. The reference to jobs is part of the fundamental mandate, not an estimate of new employment generated by the revision. ## The informational limit of the communication The external communication contains a stated direction, but not an operational timeline. It does not indicate an effective date, an implementation deadline, amounts, estimates or percentages. Nor does it specify which services or products will be affected by the simplification. Therefore, based solely on the elements provided, it is possible to describe the objective of the revision, but not to quantify the change for the Swiss export-oriented economy.
The reference to SERV has national significance because the source explicitly links its ability to respond to the needs of the Swiss export-oriented economy. The same passage places this function alongside the mandate to preserve and create jobs and promote the Swiss business location. However, the source does not provide data on the number of jobs affected, the value of exports or the cost of administrative burdens. Nor does it document any change already implemented.
The distinction between objective and result avoids attributing to the revision effects that the text does not measure. As of October 21, 2026, the available material therefore makes it possible to record a partial revision focused on three areas — access, burdens and products — and a confirmation of the fundamental mandate. Any further detail on timing, amounts, recipients or results would require information that this communication does not contain.

item.title: Return to standard time: clocks go back on October 25
item.description: Between October 24 and 25 standard time returns At 3 the hands turn back one hour 71% of Forsa respondents want to abolish the change Sleep
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Between October 24 and 25, standard time returns - At 3, the clock hands move back one hour - 71% of Forsa respondents want to abolish the time change - Sleep and energy remain the most debated points
## Key facts - When → night between Saturday 24 and Sunday 25 October - Operation → at 3, one hour back - Transition → from daylight saving time to Central European Time - Finding → 71% consider the change unnecessary - Contested objective → energy savings
### The return to standard time
LUGANO – In the night between Saturday 24 October and Sunday 25 October, at three in the morning, the clocks will be set back one hour. The transition will mark the return from daylight saving time to Central European Time, also referred to as standard time or normal time. It will be light earlier in the morning, while darkness will arrive earlier in the afternoon.
The most immediate result will be an extra hour of sleep for those who can take advantage of it. The same change, however, will mean one less hour of light in the evening. The source describes this very dual effect as the starting point for the new controversies: the time change continues to divide opinion, and many people are calling for its abolition.
The fact that people can sleep longer on Sunday has not made either the adoption of daylight saving time in spring or the return to standard time in autumn popular. A recent survey by the Forsa institute indicates that 71% of respondents consider the time change unnecessary and would like it abolished. This percentage reflects the respondents' views; it does not indicate that abolition has already been decided.
The text presents two categories of objections. Some people point to health consequences, particularly sleep disorders. Critics also question whether moving the clock hands achieves its original objective, namely energy savings. The discussion therefore starts from a concrete, date-specific operation but broadens to its effects on rest and the difficulty of demonstrating the energy benefit. Calls for abolition are reported as part of the debate, not as an outcome already formalized in the text. ## The comparison between light and consumption
### The original idea behind the time change
The reason cited by the source is the original goal of saving energy. Introducing daylight saving time in spring was supposed to reduce electricity consumption during the brighter months. The intended mechanism was straightforward: by moving the hands forward one hour, natural light would be used more and reliance on artificial lighting would be reduced.
The return in autumn makes the other side of the calendar visible. With the hands moved back, morning becomes light earlier, but darkness arrives earlier in the afternoon. Sunday offers an extra hour of sleep, while the evening loses an hour of light. The source thus presents the time change as a trade-off between different periods of daylight, not as a change limited to the clock face.
| Phase | Movement of the hands | Effect indicated by the source | |---|---|---| | Spring | One hour forward | Greater use of natural light and less reliance on artificial lighting | | Autumn | One hour back | More light in the morning, earlier darkness in the afternoon |
The comparison also clarifies why the energy goal is at the center of the criticism. The initial logic links natural light to less use of artificial lighting; however, the analyses cited in the text consider the actual benefits in terms of energy savings difficult to demonstrate. The source provides neither a percentage reduction in consumption nor an amount of electricity saved. For this reason, the benefit remains framed as the original goal and not as a quantified result.
The issue of light therefore does not coincide with that of sleep. In the first case, the question concerns the possibility of reducing artificial lighting; in the second, it concerns the rhythm and duration of rest. Keeping the two levels distinct avoids presenting the extra hour on Sunday as evidence of an energy benefit or, conversely, treating doubts about consumption as evidence of sleep disturbances. In the text, the two arguments remain connected by the movement of the clock hands, but are discussed separately. ## The sleep perspective
### Light as a regulator of the rhythm
In the debate, numerous sleep specialists argue for maintaining standard time, or winter time, because switching from one time schedule to another could alter the rhythm and duration of rest. According to this position, standard time better respects the balance between sleep and wakefulness.
Among the elements that regulate the biological clock and the sleep-wake rhythm, the source points to natural light, with particular reference to the blue component of sunlight. The experts cited believe that winter time preserves this balance better; the switch to daylight saving time, on the other hand, is associated with a possible lack of sleep.
The consequences indicated in the text are declines in concentration and performance, together with an increased risk of accidents. These effects are presented within the framework of the sleep specialists' arguments. However, the source does not provide a quantification for the individual episode, nor does it measure the extent of the disturbances or any possible increase in risk.
### What remains open
The cited survey offers an indication of respondents' orientation, while the analyses on energy and the specialists' observations concern different aspects. These elements alone do not establish either a measure of the health damage or the absence of any savings. Likewise, the difficulty of demonstrating the energy benefits does not erase the objective for which daylight saving time was introduced.
The picture presented is therefore that of a custom still in force, challenged because of possible sleep disturbances and energy benefits that are difficult to prove. The source describes the return to standard time, calls for abolition, and the positions of critics, but does not report a decision already adopted to eliminate the time change. In the text, the certain fact remains the moving of the hands of the clock at three and the switch to Central European Time.

item.title: Akira hackers steal data of 100.000 federal employees from Publica
item.description: Over 100,000 federal employees affected Data also relating to partners and children The attack on an external provider dates back to late September
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - More than 100’000 federal employees affected - Data also relating to partners and children - The attack on an external supplier dates back to late September - Akira threatens to publish or sell the data
## Key facts - What → Information theft affecting Publica - Who → Akira hacker group - Scope → Over 100’000 people - When → Late September - Data → Names, dates of birth, addresses, salaries and phone numbers - Threat → Publication or sale of the data - Development → The true scope emerged on Tuesday - RUAG precedent → It had decided to pay after the attack on the US subsidiary
The 11.00 news bulletin on October 21, 2026 reports that the information theft affecting Publica is more serious than expected. Akira’s hackers obtained the personal data of nearly all federal employees of the Confederation: over 100’000 people, including both those still working and those no longer employed by the Confederation.
The list includes officials, judges and even secret agents, as well as former federal councillors. The cyberattack targeted an external provider and dates back to late September. It had already been known for a couple of weeks, but its true scale emerged on Tuesday through articles published by media outlets in the Tamedia group.
### The data and the hackers’ demand The information in the criminals’ possession includes contact details — addresses and phone numbers —, personal details such as names and dates of birth, salary data and additional information concerning partners and children. The source does not describe a simple contact list: it brings together personal details, contact details, remuneration and family-related data.
The hackers are reportedly demanding payment of a ransom. Otherwise, they threaten to publish or sell the data. Publica has reportedly not yet informed those affected about the payment demand; in the meantime, some have already been targeted by attempted scams. ## The scope described by the report The case can be viewed through two dimensions that the report makes explicit: who is included in the group and what types of information were stolen. The first goes beyond the scope of active employees, because the theft also concerns people who are no longer employed by the Confederation. The second goes beyond basic identification: alongside names appear dates of birth, addresses, telephone numbers and salary data.
The text also mentions partners and children. The reference to the data, therefore, does not stop at the individual person included in the list. The categories indicated can be reordered as follows:
### The categories of information indicated | Area | Reported information | |---|---| | Identity | Names and dates of birth | | Contact details | Addresses and telephone numbers | | Compensation | Salary data | | Family | Information relating to partners and children |
The distinction between active employees and former employees is relevant to describing the extent of the theft, but the source does not provide a numerical breakdown between the two groups. The same applies to the occupational categories: we know that officials, judges, secret agents and former federal councillors are mentioned, but not how many belong to each group.
The available figure remains the aggregate one: more than 100’000 people, described as practically all federal employees. The list of professions serves to describe the variety of the group, not to establish a ranking or a specific figure for each role. The wording concerning family members is also limited: the report refers to other information relating to partners and children, without specifying what it is or how many people it concerns. ## The sequence of events in the case and Akira's precedents The service dates the cyberattack to the end of September and reports that it had already been known about for a couple of weeks. On Tuesday, articles published by the Tamedia group's outlets made its actual scope clear. The news report does not provide a precise day for the attack and does not identify the external provider affected: these are the limitations of the available chronological and operational reconstruction.
The passage concerning communication with the people affected is also documented. Regarding the payment demand, Publica has reportedly not yet informed those concerned. The report does state, however, that some people have already been targeted by attempted scams. It does not indicate how many there are or describe the technique used in the attempts.
### The precedent in Switzerland Akira has already carried out attacks in Switzerland, including against private companies. A year ago, the federal authorities urged companies not to comply with the hackers' demands. A few months later, RUAG, owned by the Confederation, had opted to pay, following Akira's attack against its US subsidiary.
This precedent offers a documented but limited comparison: it concerns RUAG and its US subsidiary, not Publica. In the case of the Confederation's pension fund, the source speaks of a ransom demand and threats of publication or sale, but does not indicate the amount requested or any decision on payment.
The material reported by the news service thus makes it possible to clarify the groups involved, the categories of data listed, the presence of a ransom demand and the precedent of RUAG. It does not, however, make it possible to add a numerical breakdown of the groups concerned, details about the external provider or further information about the attempted scams.
